newsitem.title: ALBANIA: ALBANIAN GOVERNMENT CALLS FOR TALKS ON CRISIS.
newsitem.headline: ALBANIAN GOVERNMENT CALLS FOR TALKS ON CRISIS.

text.p: Albania's right-wing government sought talks with the opposition socialists this week to defuse a crisis over the collapse of several high-risk pyramid investment schemes.

Widespread protests and sporadic riots have rocked the Balkan country, Europe's poorest state, for the past month as ruined investors blamed the government of Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi and demanded reimbursement.
The ruling Democrats acknowledged that hundreds of thousands of Albanians lost large sums of money when five get-rich-schemes went bust in January.
Deputy Prime Minister Tritan Shehu, the leader of the Democratic Party, called on socialist leader Rexhep Majdani to meet him on Wednesday.
But the socialists, the ex-Communist Party, have boycotted parliament since general elections last year which they said were fraudulent.

They have also refused to take part in talks on the failed pyramid schemes, which are estimated to have held $1 to $2 billion in assets and paid interest of up to 60 percent a month before they collpased.
Attention is now focused on four other major funds, which insist they are genuine business concerns, but have frozen capital investments and cut interest payments sharply.

The head of one of the country's largest investment holding companies, Vehbi Alimucaj of Vefa, appeared on television to assure investors that their money was safe and they were not linked to the pyramid schemes.

Vefa's name is present everywhere in Albania, from supermarkets and apartment blocks in the south to a large neon sign in Tirana's central square. But it has frozen deposits and is paying interest only at a greatly reduced rate.

Alimucaj said on Vefa's private channel, EuroVefa, that investors would receive their money and should not sell their deposit certificates at a discount. He said he had received $500 million in credits from foreign firms.

President Sali Berisha acknowledged on Saturday for the first time that the government committed errors in handling the pyramid collapse and had warned the public too late about the dangers of the schemes.
But he said responsibility also lay with those who had put their money into the high-interest schemes and the state had no intention of reimbursing them for their lost savings.
"We will not take this debt on our shoulders. No democratic government would do this. It would be cheating, printing money to pay and creating hyperinflation", he said.

Albania emerged from 45 years of isolationism in 1990 when a ruthless Stalinist regime fell and Berisha said the government, like the hapless pyramid investors, was still learning about the pitfalls of capitalism.
